question.text: What is the purpose of the Most Favoured Nation (MFN) clause in a DTAA?

answer.text: It grants the most favoured nation complete exemption from all taxes in India
If India signs a DTAA with another country at a lower tax rate, that lower rate may automatically apply to existing DTAA partners having the MFN clause
It allows India to impose higher tax rates on countries that do not have a DTAA with India
It restricts the number of DTAAs that India can enter into simultaneously

explanation.text: The Logic: A Most Favoured Nation (MFN) clause in a DTAA is a parity provision. It says: if one of the two contracting states later signs a DTAA with a third state and gives that third state a more favourable tax rate or scope on certain types of income (typically dividends, interest, royalties, or fees for technical services), the other contracting state in the original DTAA automatically becomes entitled to claim that better rate. It does not grant a blanket exemption, restrict treaty-making activity, or punish non-DTAA countries — it simply prevents the original partner from being left worse off than a newer partner. The Trap: An MFN clause never delivers complete exemption from Indian tax — it only equalises rates with a more-favourably-treated third country. It does not authorise India to charge higher rates on non-DTAA countries. And it does not cap how many DTAAs India can sign; India is free to enter as many DTAAs as it chooses. Note: The cited NISM Series X-B Investment Adviser Level 2 workbook pages reviewed in the audit cover general DTAA relief, beneficial rates under relevant DTAAs, and dividend beneficial-owner rates, but do not mention Most Favoured Nation or MFN clauses or automatic lower-rate parity across treaties on the pages checked. The framing above reflects general international-taxation treaty knowledge.
